what: Pilgrim's Pride is one of the world's largest chicken producers. It raises, processes and packs chicken in the United States, Mexico and the United Kingdom and Europe, where it also owns prepared-food brands. It is majority-owned by the Brazilian meat group JBS.
customers: Supermarkets, restaurant chains, foodservice distributors and food manufacturers. In Europe it sells branded prepared meats and ready meals directly to retailers.
money: Fresh and prepared chicken sold to retailers and foodservice.
Chicken plus branded prepared foods and pork products in the UK and Continental Europe.
Fresh chicken and prepared foods for the Mexican market.
moat: Scale in a commodity business is the advantage: Pilgrim's operates very large processing plants whose cost per bird is lower than smaller competitors, and it has long supply relationships with the biggest restaurant chains. Vertical integration from feed and hatchery through to processing controls quality and cost.
risks: Chicken is a commodity. Margins depend on the gap between feed costs, mostly corn and soybean meal, and chicken prices, and neither is controllable.
Free cash flow was essentially nil at $2.5M in the trailing period despite $320.4M of net income, because of capital spending and working capital.
Avian influenza outbreaks can force culls, close export markets and disrupt supply without warning.
Debt is about $3.4B against $640.2M of cash.
JBS holds a controlling stake, so minority shareholders have limited influence, and related-party arrangements deserve scrutiny.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $14.8B in 2021 to $18.5B in 2025.
The shares trade at about 0.36 times sales and 8.4 times EV/EBITDA.
Chicken is the cheapest animal protein, so consumers trade into it when beef prices rise, and beef prices have been high.
The European prepared-foods brands earn steadier margins than commodity chicken and reduce the group's cyclicality.
Seven analysts average a $33.00 target, about 19% above the current price.
watch: The spread between feed cost and chicken price. In a commodity protein business this one relationship explains almost all the variation in earnings, and watching it is more useful than watching revenue.
